exp.3:30:
It says that believers do not belong to the family of the servant woman (Hagar), but to the family of the free woman (Sarah). "Servant woman" here means a slave, and "free" describes someone who does not live under slavery. Paul concludes in this way his comparison between two sons of Abraham.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, where some were teaching that the law of Moses had to be kept in order to be accepted by God. He uses the story of Hagar and Sarah as an illustration: Ishmael was born through human effort, and Isaac through God's promise. Paul teaches that believers are children of the promise, not of the law as a way of salvation.

For today: you do not have to earn God's love through your efforts or your performance. Rest in the fact that you are his child through faith in Christ, and live with gratitude and freedom.
exp.3:14:
Here Paul asks: "Where has the joy you felt gone?" Before, they felt happy because of the gospel. The word "blessedness" in the verse means deep happiness or joy. Paul says that, if it had been possible, they would have plucked out their own eyes and given them to him. It was a way of saying that they loved him very much.

Paul writes to the Christians of Galatia, who were being influenced by teachers who were adding rules to the gospel. He reminds them of the affection they had for him when he arrived sick or weak. Some think the mention of eyes suggests a problem with eyesight, but the text does not confirm this.

For today: let us not allow our first love for Christ to grow cold. If someone tells us the truth with love, let us not see them as an enemy; rather, let us thank them for their honesty and return to the simple joy of the gospel.
exp.3:27:
It says that believers, like Isaac, are children of the promise. Isaac was born because God fulfilled what he had promised to Abraham and Sarah, not by mere human effort. "Brethren" refers to the Christians of Galatia. "Promise" is what God said he would do, and he carries it out through his own faithfulness.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, where some wanted to impose the law of Moses as the way to be accepted by God. He uses the story of Hagar and Sarah as a comparison: Ishmael was born through a human plan, and Isaac through the promise. With this, Paul shows that belonging to God comes through faith and his grace, not through works of the law. Interpreters debate some details of this comparison, but the central idea is clear.

Today you can rest in the knowledge that God received you by his promise and his grace, not by your performance. Live thankful, without fear of losing your place in his family.
exp.3:23:
Paul says that the story of Hagar and Sarah has a deeper meaning. An allegory means that real events also serve as a picture of another teaching. The two women represent two covenants, or agreements God makes with his people. Hagar, the servant, is connected with Mount Sinai, where the law was given, and her children are born to bondage, that is, slavery.

Paul writes to the Christians of Galatia, who were being pressured to keep the law of Moses in order to be accepted by God. He uses this well-known story to show that depending on the law leads to a life of slavery, while God's promise brings freedom.

For today: you do not have to earn God's love through effort and lists of rules. Trust in the promise of Christ and live with gratitude, as a free child.
exp.3:25:
It says there is a Jerusalem "above," that is, a heavenly Jerusalem, and that she is free. Furthermore, Paul calls her "the mother of us all," that is, of all who believe in Christ. The words "But" and "Jerusalem" appear as they do in the verse above.

Paul writes to the Galatians, who were being tempted to return to the law of Moses in order to feel accepted by God. He uses the story of Hagar and Sarah as an allegory. Hagar represents the covenant of Sinai and slavery; Sarah represents the promise and freedom. Paul wants to show that believers belong to the free family of God.

For today: you do not have to earn God's love through effort or through fear. In Christ you are already a son or daughter, with a place in his family. Live thankfully, obeying him out of love and not in order to be accepted.
exp.1:1:
Paul says that he went up to Jerusalem because God revealed it to him, or led him to do so. There he presented the gospel he preaches among non-Jews (the "Gentiles"). He did this privately with those who seemed to be important, that is, the leaders of greatest standing. His aim was to make sure he did not run in vain: that his work would not be wasted. "Communicated" here means "explained."

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, who were confused by those who said that non-Jewish believers had to be circumcised. He defends that his message did not come from men, and that the leaders in Jerusalem added nothing to it. Some understand that he was not doubting his message, but wanted to show unity. Others see a real concern for the fruit of his labor.

Today, being humble does not mean keeping silent about what we believe. We can share our convictions with mature brothers and sisters, listen, and seek unity, without changing the truth of grace in Christ.
exp.2:2:
Paul asks a sharp question: "Are ye so foolish?" He means: are they really so lacking in understanding? He reminds them that their Christian life began through the Spirit, that is, through God's work in them. So why do they now think they can reach maturity by the flesh, that is, by human effort and by keeping rules?

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. Some were teaching them that, in addition to believing in Christ, they had to keep the law of Moses. Paul, like a worried father, reminds them that they received the Spirit by hearing with faith, not by works.

Today we can fall into the same thing: believing that God accepted us by grace, yet living as if it now depended on our performance. Every day, trust God and ask him for his Spirit to grow.
exp.5:12:
They say that those who pressure the Galatians to be circumcised do not even keep the whole law themselves. What they want is to boast, that is, to take pride that they succeeded in getting others to follow their practice. "Flesh" here refers to the body marked by circumcision, an outward sign.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, who were being influenced by teachers who required circumcision in order to be accepted by God. Paul corrects them firmly, and he himself writes this part in his own hand, with large letters. He maintains that salvation is found in the cross of Christ, not in outward rites.

For today: examine your motives. It is easy to want others to follow our religious customs so that we feel superior. Instead, let your pride rest only in what Christ did for you on the cross, and treat others with humility and grace.
exp.2:9:
Galatians 3:10 says that those who rely on keeping the law to be accepted by God are under a curse. Paul quotes Scripture: cursed is everyone who does not continue in all the things the law requires, to do them. "Curse" means condemnation or punishment from God. "Continue" means to keep on steadily. The law demands complete obedience, not partial obedience.

Paul is writing to the Galatians, who were being pressured to add the works of the law to faith in Christ. He quotes Deuteronomy 27:26. His argument is that no one keeps everything, so the law cannot save. That is why he insists that the blessing promised to Abraham comes through faith.

For today: do not try to earn God's favor through good behavior. Humbly acknowledge your failures, trust in Christ, and then obey out of gratitude, not out of fear.
exp.0:19:
It says that Paul solemnly affirms that what he is writing is true. "Behold" is like saying "look carefully," and "before God" means he speaks as if God himself were watching him. "I lie not" is plain: he is not exaggerating or making anything up.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. Some were questioning him and saying that his message came only from the apostles in Jerusalem. He answers that he received the gospel directly from Jesus Christ, and he tells how, after three years, he visited Peter and saw James, but no other apostles. That is why he swears that his account is true. His authority as an apostle was at stake.

For today: watch your words as if you were speaking before God, because you are. Be honest, even when no one can check what you say.
exp.0:14:
He says God decided, by his own will, to act in Paul's life. The word "pleased" in the verse conveys that it was God's good pleasure to do so. The phrase "separated me" means that God set Paul apart for a purpose, and this was from before he was born. Furthermore, God called him "by his grace," meaning as a gift that Paul did not earn. The sentence continues in the next verse: God was willing to reveal his Son in him so that he would proclaim him among the non-Jews.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. Some were questioning his authority and his message. That is why he tells how he used to persecute the church and was very zealous for the Jewish traditions. His change was not his own idea or a teaching of men, but the work of God.

For today: no one is beyond the reach of God's grace, whether because of their past or their mistakes. If God has called you, trust that he is still working in your life with purpose, and respond with humility and gratitude.
exp.5:1:
It says that believers should help one another carry their burdens. "Bear" means to carry together, to help one another endure. "Fulfil" means to carry out in practice. So, by helping others, one lives out what Christ taught.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. Just before this, he speaks of gently restoring someone who has fallen into a fault. Then he warns against thinking oneself superior and asks that each person examine his own life. Many understand "the law of Christ" to refer to the love that Jesus commanded and lived, though some explain it in other ways.

Today you can notice someone close to you who is tired, sick, or going through a difficulty, and offer them something concrete: listening to them, praying with them, cooking for them, or accompanying them to an appointment. Truly helping starts with a simple step.
exp.2:16:
Paul says that God made a covenant with Abraham, and that this covenant was confirmed beforehand in relation to Christ. The law came 430 years later, and it cannot set aside that covenant or make the promise void. Here "covenant" means the agreement God made, and "disannul" means to cancel or make something no longer valid.

Paul writes to the Christians of Galatia, who were being influenced to believe that they had to keep the law of Moses in order to be accepted by God. To answer them, he uses the example of a human agreement, which no one changes once it has been confirmed. The 430 years is a figure Paul takes from the biblical tradition (Exodus 12:40), and some scholars discuss how it is calculated.

For today: you do not need to earn God's love through your own effort. His promise in Christ is firm. Rest in his faithfulness and obey him out of gratitude, not out of fear.
exp.3:5:
This verse says that, since we are already children of God, he placed the Spirit of his Son Jesus in our hearts. That Spirit leads us to cry out, that is, to call out with confidence: "Abba, Father." "Abba" is an Aramaic word that was used affectionately to mean "daddy" or "father."

Paul writes to the Christians of Galatia, who were being tempted to return to the law as the way to please God. He reminds them that Christ came to redeem us and to give us adoption as children. Because of this, we no longer live as servants, but as children and heirs.

Today you can come near to God without fear or pretense. When you pray, speak to him like a beloved child speaking with his Father, even if you feel weak or do not know what to say. The Spirit accompanies you in that prayer.
exp.0:6:
Paul says that there is really no "another gospel," that is, no other true good news. What does exist are people who trouble you, meaning they unsettle you and fill you with confusion. They would pervert the gospel, which means twisting and changing it so that it becomes different from what it is.

Paul writes to the churches in Galatia. He is astonished that they are turning away so quickly from the grace they received. From the rest of the letter, it is clear that these teachers were adding requirements from the law to faith in Christ. Some scholars debate the exact details of that group, but the central problem was changing the message of grace.

Today, when we hear a teaching, let us compare it with what the Bible says about Jesus. If it adds burdens or takes away grace, it is wise to examine it calmly, with prayer and with other mature believers.
exp.3:4:
He says that Jesus came to "redeem," that is, to buy back the freedom of those who lived under the law, just as a slave was ransomed by paying the price for him. The purpose was that we might receive the "adoption of sons": to be accepted into God's family with all the rights of a son.

The apostle Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, which were being pressured to again depend on the law in order to feel accepted by God. He reminds them that they used to be like children under guardians, but God sent his Son, born of a woman and subject to the law, to free them from that slavery and make them sons.

For today: you do not have to earn God's love through effort or fear. If you trust in Christ, you already are a son or daughter. Today, pray to God as to a Father who receives you with affection.
exp.4:24:
If we have received new life from the Holy Spirit, this verse says, we should also let his guidance shape the way we live day to day. "Live" refers to the spiritual life that God gives. "Walk" means that our daily conduct should keep the same pace as the Spirit.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, writing to the churches in Galatia. Earlier he spoke of the fruit of the Spirit, such as gentleness and self-control, and of those who have put to death the flesh, that is, who have stopped obeying their selfish desires. Then he warns against conceit, provoking others, and envy. In this way Paul wants faith to be visible in how we treat other people.

For today: before you react with anger or envy, stop and pray. Ask yourself, "What would someone guided by the Spirit do here?" Then take one concrete step of patience or kindness.
exp.0:21:
He says that Paul was not personally known, that is, "by sight," to the Christian churches of Judea, which were "in Christ," meaning joined to Jesus through faith. The word "á" carries an accent because of older spelling; today it would be written as "a."

In this letter Paul argues that he received the gospel directly from Christ, not from the apostles. After his conversion, he spent years in Arabia, Damascus, Syria, and Cilicia, and he visited Jerusalem only briefly. That is why he explains that the churches of Judea did not know him in person; they had only heard of his change. Some interpreters see here that his message did not depend on the approval of those churches.

For today: a transformed life speaks for itself. Even when others do not know us closely, our change in Christ can lead people to give glory to God. Let us live with sincerity, without seeking fame.
exp.3:6:
This verse says that the believer no longer lives as a slave, but as a child of God. And if he is a child, he also receives an inheritance from God, and receives it through Christ. "Servant" here means slave, and "heir" is the one who receives what the Father has prepared for his children.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, who is writing to the churches of Galatia. Some were beginning to depend again on the law to feel accepted by God. Paul reminds them that Christ redeemed them, that God adopted them, and that the Spirit gives them the confidence to cry out to God in a close and familiar way.

For today: when you feel guilty or think you must earn God's love, remember who you are. You do not pray like a slave who fears, but like a beloved child. Come near to God with confidence, and obey him out of love, not out of fear.
exp.2:26:
The explanation says that everyone who was baptized into Christ has "put on" Christ. The phrase "have been baptized" means "you have been baptized," and "have put on" means that they have clothed themselves with Christ as a garment. It is an image of identity: whoever believes in Jesus is united with Him and stands before God in Him.

The apostle Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, who were being pressured to keep the law of Moses in order to be accepted by God. Before, the law was like a guardian, who cared for and guided until Christ came. Now, through faith, all are children of God. Christians interpret the exact role of baptism here in different ways, but all see that it speaks of being united with Christ.

Today you can remember that your worth does not depend on your background, your achievements, or your position. If you are in Christ, treat other believers as equals, and live each day as someone who wears the character of Jesus.
exp.4:12:
He says that God called us to be free, that is, free from trying to earn his favor by keeping rules such as circumcision. But that freedom is not permission to do whatever selfishness asks. Giving the flesh an opportunity means giving a pretext or an open door to selfish desires. Instead, Paul says that we should serve one another through love.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, where some teachers insisted that believers had to be circumcised to be accepted by God. Paul maintains that Christ, on the cross, already gave us freedom. But he also warns that this freedom can be twisted and cause quarrels among brothers and sisters, as the following verse shows.

For today: before deciding something you can do, ask yourself whether it will help or harm someone close to you. Use your freedom to serve, for example, by quietly helping someone who needs it this week.
exp.0:22:
They did not know Paul personally. They had only heard a report: the man who once persecuted them was now preaching the same faith he had tried to destroy. The phrase "preaches the faith" means that he proclaims the gospel, that is, what Christians believe about Jesus.

Paul is speaking in his letter to the Galatians. He maintains that he received the gospel from God and not from the apostles. For this reason he tells how, after his conversion, he spent time in Syria and Cilicia, far from Judea. The churches of Judea only learned of his change through the testimony of others, and the next verse says that because of this they glorified God.

For today: never give up on a person, not even on yourself. God can transform lives in a real and visible way. And when you see a change in someone, instead of distrusting endlessly, you can thank God, as those churches did.
exp.4:13:
Paul says that the whole law of God is summed up and fulfilled in one sentence: to love your neighbor as yourself. The word "this" here is an older way of saying "this one," and "neighbor" means anyone we have close to us. "Is fulfilled" means that the purpose of the law is accomplished through love.

Paul is writing to the Christians of Galatia, who were being pressured by teachers who wanted to impose the law of Moses on them. He reminds them that they were called to freedom, but that freedom is not for living selfishly; it is for serving one another through love. If they bite and devour each other, they will destroy one another.

Today we can ask ourselves before we act or speak: "Is this love toward the other person?" For example, instead of criticizing someone in church or in the family, we can choose to serve them with a concrete and patient act.
exp.2:19:
It says that a mediator always acts between two parties, not just one. By contrast, God is one. Here "mediator" refers to the one who stood between God and the people when the law was given (Moses, according to most readers). This verse is famous for being difficult, and it has been interpreted in many ways.

Paul is writing to the Galatians, who were tempted to depend on the law to be accepted by God. He explains that the law came through angels and through a mediator, with two parties involved. The promise to Abraham, by contrast, came directly from God, who gave it by his grace alone. For that reason the promise carries more weight and is not nullified by the law.

For today: rest in what God promised and did for you in Christ, and not in your performance. Serve God with gratitude, not to earn his love.
exp.1:9:
The only thing the leaders in Jerusalem asked of Paul was that he not forget the poor. And Paul says that this very thing was what he was already eagerly working to do. "Eager" here means diligent, willing, and attentive.

Paul speaks of this in his letter to the Galatians. He tells how James, Peter, and John accepted his message and his mission to the non-Jews without adding requirements. There was only this one request. Many understand it to refer to the poor among the believers in Jerusalem, although the text does not specify this. Paul mentions it to show that the gospel of grace and generosity go together.

For today: true faith shows itself in practical care for those in need. Think of a person or family close to you who is in need, and help them this week with something concrete.
exp.5:13:
Paul says that he will never take pride in anything except the cross of Jesus Christ. Where a sentence would explain an unusual word, I have instead spoken of the boasting itself: to take pride or boast in something. In this verse, the word that presses or compels people is replaced with a plain description: some teachers were pressing the believers to be circumcised. Through that cross, the world with its values lost its power over Paul, and he also stopped being tied to that world.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. Some teachers were pressing non-Jewish believers to be circumcised, so that they would look good before others and avoid rejection. Paul answers that it is not about outward marks or about boasting in religious achievements. What counts is the new creation that God makes in the one who trusts in Christ.

Today we can ask ourselves what we tend to boast about: success, image, good religious behavior. We can hand over that need for approval and rest in what Christ has done for us, letting his love be our greatest confidence.
exp.3:17:
It says that it is good to have a passionate interest, or "zeal," in what is good, and that this should be constant. Being "zealously affected in a good thing" means being fervent in pursuing what is good. The words "ye" and "you" refer to the same readers, and "affected" means being moved or stirred toward a goal.

Paul writes to the Galatians, who were being influenced by teachers who courted them with self-serving motives: they wanted the Galatians to follow them. Paul reminds them that his affection for them does not depend on his being present: it is sincere and constant. At the same time, he shows his heartfelt concern as a father worried about their faith.

For today: examine why you serve or get excited about things. Ask yourself whether your enthusiasm for doing good is constant, even when no one sees you, and whether it seeks the good of others or only your own benefit.
exp.3:2:
This verse says that, before Christ, we were like children who lived as servants. "Rudiments" means the basic or elementary teachings, like the alphabet of the spiritual life. "Under the elements" can refer to human rules, to the law seen as an early stage, or to spiritual powers; scholars interpret it in several ways.

The apostle Paul is writing to the Christians of Galatia. Some were wanting to return to depending on the law of Moses to be accepted by God. Paul uses the picture of an heir who is still a minor, who does not yet enjoy his inheritance because he is under guardians. In this way he explains that this stage has already passed with the coming of Christ.

For today: do not live your faith as a list of rules to earn God's favor. In Christ you are a son or daughter, not a servant. Obey out of trust and love, not out of fear.
exp.0:12:
Paul reminds the Galatians of what they already knew about his past life. When he practiced Judaism, he persecuted the church of God beyond measure, meaning in an extreme way, and tried to destroy it. His way of living at that time was known to them.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, where some were teaching a different gospel. He insists that his message did not come from people, but from Jesus Christ himself. He mentions his past to show that he could not have invented or learned this gospel from others: before, he was an enemy of the faith. Only an encounter with Christ could change him.

For today: no one is too far away for God to transform. If you have a past you are ashamed of, offer it to God with humility. And if you know someone who seems closed to faith, keep praying for that person with hope.
exp.4:19:
This verse continues the list of the "works of the flesh." It mentions worshiping other gods or things in place of the true God (idolatry), practices of witchcraft or the use of hidden powers (sorcery), and attitudes that damage relationships: hatred, quarrels, jealousy, anger, rivalries, and divisions. The word "heresies" here refers to groups or factions that split apart out of stubbornness, rather than to false doctrines in the technical sense.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, who were being pressured to return to the law as the way of life. He reminds them that whoever is guided by the Spirit does not live under that pressure, and he shows them what life looks like without the Spirit.

Today we can ask ourselves which attitude dominates our relationships: jealousy, anger, or rivalry? Ask the Spirit to guide you, and seek to be reconciled with someone this week.
exp.4:23:
This verse says that those who belong to Christ have "crucified the flesh." The "flesh" is our human nature inclined toward what is wrong. The "affections" are the passions and disordered desires, and the "lusts" are the strong desires to do what God does not approve. To crucify is to put them to death, to reject them as someone who no longer gives them command.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. He has just contrasted the works of the flesh with the fruit of the Spirit. He wants them to understand that belonging to Christ changes the way one lives. Then he encourages them to walk in the Spirit and not fall into vain conceit or envy.

For today: when a desire arises that pulls you away from God, such as anger, envy, or pride, do not feed it. Pray and decide to obey the Spirit in that moment, trusting that Christ gives you strength.
exp.5:7:
This verse uses the image of sowing and reaping. A person who sows to their own flesh, that is, who lives for their desires and selfishness, will reap decay, something that spoils and ends in ruin. A person who sows to the Spirit, that is, who lives guided by God, will reap life that never ends.

Paul is writing to the Christians of Galatia. He has just asked them to support those who teach them the word, and he warns them that God cannot be mocked. He reminds them that our choices have consequences. What follows encourages them not to grow weary of doing good.

For today: think about one small decision you make this week, such as how you use your time, your money, or your words. Ask yourself whether it is a seed for your own desires or for the Spirit. Choose one concrete action today, such as praying, forgiving, or helping someone, and do not lose heart if the harvest takes time.
exp.4:25:
It says we should not desire "vain glory," that is, the applause and recognition that are worth nothing. When we seek it, we end up provoking and challenging others, and envying one another, feeling resentment at what others have or achieve. The word "covetous" here speaks of a disordered desire to be admired.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, writing to the churches of Galatia. He has just explained that living in the Spirit is different from living according to the flesh, and that this produces fruit such as love, peace, and patience. This verse shows a concrete sign of living according to the flesh: rivalry and envy among brothers and sisters. Paul calls them to walk in a different way.

Today, when you see that someone receives a compliment or an achievement that you wanted, pray for that person and thank God for them. In this way envy loses its strength and love grows.
exp.2:4:
Paul asks the Galatians a simple question: God gave them his Spirit and was doing miracles among them. Did he do this because they kept the law of Moses, or because they heard the message and believed?

The idea of "hearing with faith" means listening to the gospel and trusting in it.

Paul writes this letter to the churches of Galatia. Some teachers were telling them that, in addition to believing in Christ, they had to keep the law, and Paul corrects that mistake. He reminds them of what they already experienced: they received the Spirit when they believed, not through their own effort. Afterward he will use Abraham as an example.

Today we can remember that our relationship with God begins and grows through trusting in Christ, not through trying to earn his favor. When you feel tired of trying to be enough, listen again to the gospel and rest in his grace.
exp.0:0:
Paul presents himself as an apostle, that is, someone sent out with a mission and with authority. He makes clear that his calling did not come from men or through any man, but from Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, a region in Asia Minor. At the beginning he defends his authority, because some were questioning his message. Later in the letter it becomes clear that he was speaking about the gospel of grace. Here he supports that message by pointing to the resurrection of Jesus. Exactly who was challenging him is explained in several ways, but the letter shows that there was pressure to change the gospel.

Today we can ask where what we believe comes from. Rather than following trends or human opinions, let us seek what God has revealed in Jesus Christ and in his Word, and live with that confidence.
exp.0:10:
Paul tells the brothers in Galatia that he wants them to know something clearly: the gospel he preached does not come from human origin. "Not after man" means it was not invented, devised, or adapted by people.

Paul is writing to the churches of Galatia, who were being confused by those who taught a different message. Earlier he has said that he is not trying to please people, but to serve Christ. Now he defends that his message comes from God, and in the verses that follow he explains that he received it through a revelation of Jesus Christ.

Today we can ask ourselves whether what we believe comes from the Word of God or from what is convenient, popular, or pleasing. It is worth returning to the Scriptures and measuring everything by what Christ has revealed.
exp.2:8:
This verse says that the people who trust God, that is, "those of faith," receive God's blessing together with Abraham. Their blessing is not something they earned, but something they receive as believers. Abraham is called "faithful" because he believed what God told him.

Paul is writing to the Christians of Galatia, who were being influenced to think that they had to keep the law of Moses in order to please God. Paul reminds them that God had already promised to bless all the nations through Abraham, long before the law existed. Therefore, the blessing comes through faith and not through one's own effort.

Today you can rest in the fact that God accepts you because you trust in Christ, not because of your achievements. When you feel inadequate, trust again in his promise and live thankful, not afraid.
exp.4:8:
It says that a small amount of yeast, which is what makes bread rise, ends up making the whole dough swell. The word for "making it rise" in the source, as the explanation puts it, means to ferment, so the point is that something small can affect the whole batch.

Paul writes to the Galatians, who were doing well in the faith, but some teachers were persuading them that they had to be circumcised to be accepted by God. The explanation says that the word for "hindered" means to hinder, that is, to get in the way. Paul fears that this teaching, though it may seem minor, will contaminate the truth of the gospel of grace. Interpreters debate whether the "leaven" is the false doctrine or the people who teach it; both ideas fit the text.

Today, let us not take lightly ideas or small habits that drift away from the truth. Let us examine carefully what we hear, and let the grace of Christ be our foundation.
exp.2:11:
What it says: The law does not work through trust in God, but through obedience. Its principle is: whoever carries out its commands will live by them. The word "also" here means "in addition," and the phrase "carries them out" means "fulfills them." In other words, the law asks for doing, not only for believing.

Context: Paul writes to the Galatians, who were being pressured to add the law of Moses to their faith in Christ. He cites Leviticus 18:5 to show that the law demands complete obedience, and that no one keeps it perfectly. That is why, he says, justification comes through faith, and Christ freed us from that curse.

For today: Do not try to earn God's love by your good behavior. Trust in what Christ has already done for you, and let that gratitude lead you to obey him with joy, not with fear.
exp.2:3:
Paul asks: "Have you experienced so many things for nothing?" The word "suffered" can refer to persecution or to everything they went through. "Yet" means "but." He adds: "if it really was in vain," leaving a door of hope open.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. Some teachers were telling them that, to be complete, they had to add the works of the law to their faith in Christ. Paul, concerned and firm, reminds them that they received the Spirit by believing, not by keeping rules.

For today: do not think you grow with God only through effort and rules. You began by trusting in the grace of Christ; keep walking in that same path, and let the Spirit sustain you each day.
exp.1:0:
Paul says that, after fourteen years, he went back up to Jerusalem with Barnabas and also took Titus with him. The words "I went up again" show that he had already been there before. The fourteen years are counted from his conversion or from his first visit; scholars interpret this in different ways.

Paul is speaking in his letter to the churches of Galatia. He argues that the gospel he preaches did not come from men but from God. He mentions this visit to show that his message to the Gentiles was the same as that of the apostles. Titus, a Greek believer, would be a living proof of that truth.

For today: we do not need to add human requirements to the grace of God. Even so, it is wise to share what we believe with other mature believers, so that we walk in unity and do not run in vain.
exp.0:23:
The explanation says that the people in the churches of Judea praised God because of what He had done in Paul. The word "glorified" means that they recognized God as the author of the change and gave Him honor. The phrase in the verse can be understood as "because of me" or "because of what God did in me."

Paul speaks in his letter to the Galatians. He argues that the gospel he preaches comes from God and not from the apostles in Jerusalem. He recounts that, after his conversion, he was not personally known to the churches of Judea. They only heard that the former persecutor was now proclaiming the faith. His transformation was so real that it caused gratitude, not distrust.

For today: when God changes your life, or someone else's, make sure the praise does not stop with you. Let your testimony lead others to give thanks to God, and rejoice sincerely when He transforms a difficult person.
exp.3:13:
Paul reminds the Galatians that, although he had a physical trial that could have led them to reject him, they did not despise him. On the contrary, they welcomed him with honor, as a messenger sent by God, even as Christ himself.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, who were now being led astray by false teachers. He reminds them of the affection they once had so that they can see how much they have changed. We do not know for certain what his illness was; some think of a problem with his eyes, but this is not certain.

Today we can learn to value people for the message of God they bring and not for their appearance or their weaknesses. We can also be thankful to those who taught us the faith, and not forget the love with which we once received the truth.
exp.2:28:
This verse says that whoever belongs to Christ is also a descendant of Abraham. Therefore, according to the promise God made to Abraham, that person is an heir. "Seed" means descendants, and an "heir" is someone who receives what was promised to them.

Paul writes to the Christians in Galatia, where some were teaching that one had to keep the law of Moses to be part of God's people. Paul answers that faith in Christ is enough. He had already said that in Christ all are one, regardless of origin, social standing, or sex. Here he concludes that this union with Christ gives a share in the promise made to Abraham.

For today: you do not need to earn your place through merit or compare yourself with others. If you trust in Christ, you already belong to God's family. Treat your brothers and sisters in the faith as equals, regardless of their background or position.
exp.3:29:
Paul asks what the Scripture says, and he quotes what Sarah asked of Abraham: "Cast out the bondwoman and her son." The bondwoman is Hagar and her son is Ishmael. The son of the bondwoman will not receive the inheritance together with Isaac, the son of the freewoman, Sarah.

Paul writes to the Galatians, who were being pressured to return to the law of Moses in order to be accepted by God. He uses the story of Abraham as an illustration: Ishmael was born through human effort, and Isaac through God's promise (Genesis 21:10). For Paul, the inheritance comes through the promise, not through works. Some interpreters debate the details of this allegory, but its central point is clear.

For today: do not try to earn God's love through efforts or merits. Rest in his promise, and let go of everything that makes you feel enslaved to guilt or to appearances.
exp.5:3:
This verse says that each person should honestly examine their own work and conduct. If in doing so they find something good, they can rejoice in that very thing, without comparing themselves to others. "Work" means what a person does; "pride" here refers to a healthy sense of accomplishment or satisfaction, not to fame.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. He speaks of helping one another with burdens and of not thinking themselves better than others. Just before this, he warns that whoever thinks himself to be something is deceiving himself. He then adds that each person will bear their own load. Some see here a balance between helping others and taking responsibility for oneself.

For today: before you criticize or compare yourself to someone, take a few minutes to ask God how you are doing. Give thanks for what is good, correct what needs correcting, and rejoice without competing.
exp.0:9:
Paul asks questions to make something clear: is he trying to win the favor of people or of God? He says that if he were still trying to please men, he would not be a servant of Christ.

Pablo escribe a las iglesias de Galacia... — translated below.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, where some were preaching a different gospel. It seems they accused him of softening the message to be liked. So he reminds them that his message does not change according to what people think and that it comes from Christ, as he explains in the verses that follow.

Today we might ask ourselves: whom do I want to please when I speak or make decisions? Being kind to everyone is good, but we must not change the truth or our faithfulness to Christ just to be accepted.
exp.3:11:
Paul pleads with them tenderly: "Brothers, I beg you, become as I am, for I became as you are." He also says they did him no "wrong," that is, no offense or personal harm.

Paul writes to the Galatians, who were returning to religious practices such as keeping days, months, and years, as if that would bring them salvation. Paul, a Jew, had stopped depending on the law to be made righteous before God, and he identified himself with them, who were not Jews. He reminds them that there is no resentment between them, and he appeals to the good relationship they once had. Some think he means that they should live free from the law as he does; the text does not clarify this further.

For today: when we need to correct someone, let us do it with gentleness, remembering the relationship and without resentment, seeking their good and not winning an argument.
exp.1:5:
Paul speaks about the leaders of the church in Jerusalem, the ones who had a reputation for being important. He says that whatever they were before does not matter to him, because God does not look at outward appearance or at a person's standing. He adds that those leaders did not add anything to his message.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia to defend the gospel of grace. Some were saying that his message came secondhand and needed the approval of Jerusalem. Paul tells how he met with them, but that they did not correct his message; on the contrary, they recognized his calling to the non-Jewish peoples. He does not say this with contempt toward them, but to defend the truth.

Today we can learn not to measure faith by someone's fame, position, or popularity. It is good to examine every teaching in the light of God's Word, and to remember that he looks at the heart.
exp.5:11:
It says that those who want to look good to people, judging by human and outward standards, pressure the Galatians to be circumcised. They do this only to avoid being persecuted for preaching the cross of Christ. The verse's word "constrain" means to force or press hard.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. Some teachers taught that non-Jewish believers had to be circumcised to be accepted by God. Paul says that they were seeking approval and security, and that they did not even keep the whole law themselves. He, on the other hand, boasts only in the cross of Christ.

For today: examine whether you sometimes stay silent or change your faith out of fear of rejection. Ask God for the courage to live out the message of the cross simply, with love, and without seeking applause.
exp.3:0:
Paul says that an heir, as long as he is still a child, does not stand out at all from a servant, even though he is in fact the owner of everything his father has. The word "stand out" in this verse does not appear in your English text, so I will not explain it here. Even though everything belongs to him, in practice he lives under rules and cannot decide anything about his inheritance.

Paul writes to the churches in Galatia, who were drawn toward returning to the law of Moses as a requirement for being accepted by God. He uses this everyday picture to show that the time under the law was a stage of preparation, until Christ came. Scholars debate exactly what is meant by the elementary forces of the world, but the central point is clear: that stage has already passed.

Today, if you trust in Christ, you are a child of God and not a fearful servant. Live with the confidence of a beloved child, not trying to earn God's affection through religious effort.
exp.3:20:
Paul asks the Galatians a direct question. They wanted to live "under the law," that is, under Moses' system of rules, in order to be accepted by God. Paul asks them whether they have truly listened to what the law itself teaches, since they defend it but do not understand its full message.

Paul writes with the heart of a father, concerned and even deeply troubled for them. Some teachers were telling them they must add the law to faith in Christ. That is why Paul uses the law itself, the account of Abraham, to show them that God's promise travels another road: the road of faith.

For today: before you burden yourself with rules to earn God's favor, listen again to what his Word says about his grace. Rest in what Christ has already done.
exp.2:12:
He says that Christ "redeemed" us, that is, he rescued us by paying a price, from the "curse of the law." That curse was the condemnation the law pronounced on those who did not keep it perfectly. Christ took it upon himself: he was "made a curse" for us. Paul quotes Deuteronomy 21:23, which said that whoever was hanged on a tree was under a curse. A "tree" here means a cross or a wooden beam.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, where some were teaching that they had to keep the law to be accepted by God. He answers that no one is made righteous by the law, but that the righteous live by faith. Christ bore the condemnation so that the blessing promised to Abraham would also reach the non-Jews.

Today, if guilt weighs on you or you feel you never measure up, remember that Christ has already borne that condemnation. Trust in what he did, and live thankful, not in fear.
exp.0:13:
Paul says that in Judaism he was advancing ahead of many young men of his own age and nation. The word "profited" in the verse means making progress or advancing. "Zealous" means very eager and passionate. The "traditions of my fathers" were the religious teachings and customs inherited from his ancestors.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. Some teachers were questioning his authority and teaching a different gospel. For that reason he recalls his past: he did not receive the message from other men, but from Jesus Christ. If anyone had reason to follow only tradition, it was he, yet God transformed him.

For today: we can have great religious zeal and still be mistaken. Let us examine our customs and efforts in the light of Christ, and ask God for humility to follow Him, not only what we have always done.
exp.3:28:
It says that, just as in the past Ishmael, the son born through human effort ("according to the flesh"), persecuted Isaac, the son born through God's promise ("according to the Spirit"), the same thing is happening now.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, where some teachers wanted believers to keep the law of Moses in order to be accepted by God. Paul uses the story of Hagar and Sarah as an illustration: whoever trusts in their own works is like the son of the slave woman; whoever trusts in the promise is like Isaac. Genesis mentions Ishmael mocking Isaac; Paul interprets this as persecution.

For today: do not be surprised if living by grace brings you criticism, even from religious people. Rest in the fact that you are a child of God through his promise, not through your merits, and respond with patience and love.
exp.3:26:
She says that the barren woman, the one who had no children and was forsaken, should rejoice and cry out with joy, because she will have more children than the one who has a husband.

Paul writes to the Galatians, who were tempted to return to the law of Moses to be accepted by God. He quotes Isaiah 54:1, a promise to Jerusalem in exile, and applies it to the Jerusalem above, the mother of believers. Sarah, though barren, bore Isaac, the child of the promise. Paul wants to show that God's family is born through the promise and not through human effort.

For today: if you feel empty or without fruit, remember that God can give life where you see no way out. Trust in his promise and not in your own strength.
exp.4:14:
It says that if believers bite and devour one another, like animals fighting, they will end up destroying each other. The images of biting and devouring describe fighting, harsh criticism, and mistreatment. Being consumed means to be finished off or wiped out.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. He speaks to them about the freedom they have in Christ, but warns them not to use it for selfishness. It seems there were divisions and arguments among them, and the apostle reminds them that love for one's neighbor sums up the law. Right after this, he calls them to walk in the Spirit.

For today: before criticizing or responding in anger to a brother or sister, stop and ask yourself whether your words build up or tear down. Ask the Spirit to help you speak with love and seek peace.
exp.0:16:
Paul says that, after God called him, he did not go up right away to Jerusalem to see those who were already apostles before him. Instead, he went away into Arabia and then returned again to Damascus.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, where some doubted his authority. He defends that he received the gospel directly from Christ, not from human leaders. Where he stayed in Arabia and what he did there is not explained in the text; some think it was a time of prayer and reflection, but that is a guess.

For today: before rushing into serving or offering opinions, it is wise to set aside time to be alone with God, to listen to his Word, and to let him confirm our faith. The counsel of others helps, but our foundation is Christ himself.
exp.3:9:
Paul says that the Galatians "observe" or keep careful watch over certain days, months, times, and years. He is referring to religious celebrations and calendars that they had begun to keep as though they were necessary.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, concerned that some were trying to bring them under Jewish law. It is not certain whether he means only Jewish festivals or also pagan customs; scholars understand it in several ways. What is clear is that Paul fears his work among them may have been in vain, and he addresses them affectionately as brothers.

For today: examine whether any religious habit has become a burden or a way of trying to earn God's favor. Days and practices can help us worship, but our relationship with God rests on his grace, not on keeping a calendar.
exp.4:17:
This verse says that if the Holy Spirit is the one guiding us, we are no longer living under the law. "Led" means carried along, guided by the hand. "Under the law" means living under its demand and its condemnation, like someone trying to earn God's approval by keeping rules.

Paul writes to the Christians of Galatia, who were being pressured to return to the obligations of the law of Moses. He shows them that the Christian life is not sustained by rules, but by walking in the Spirit, who gives us strength to resist the sinful desires of the flesh. The verses that follow describe those works of the flesh.

For today: before deciding something, or when you feel tempted, pray and ask for the Spirit's guidance. Do not live only to check off a list, nor to do whatever you feel like. Seek a daily relationship with God, and let Him shape your character.
exp.4:5:
It says that, for someone united with Christ, being Jewish (circumcised) or not Jewish (uncircumcised) gives no advantage before God. What counts is faith that works through love. The word "love" in this verse is the one used throughout, and it means the same thing here as it does elsewhere in the passage. "Works" means that faith is active and shows itself in actions.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. Some teachers were telling them that, to be accepted by God, they had to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses. Paul answers that trusting in that means turning away from grace. True faith does not stop at a religious rule, but lives and shows itself in love.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we trust in our customs or religious achievements to feel accepted. God receives us through faith in Christ. That faith shows itself in simple things: forgiving, serving, helping, and treating others with kindness.
exp.2:6:
The explanation says that Abraham's true children are not those who are so by blood or by keeping the law, but those who trust God as he did. "Know" means "understand" or "hold as certain," and in the verse above the phrase "they which are of faith" refers to those who live by trusting God.

Paul writes to the Christians in Galatia, who were being influenced by people who said that, to belong to God's people, they had to keep the law of Moses. Paul reminds them that they received the Spirit by believing, not by keeping rules. Abraham was declared righteous because of his faith, so God's family is recognized by faith.

Today we can rest in the fact that God accepts us because we trust in Christ, not because of our performance. This frees us from the pressure of earning his love and unites us with believers from every culture.
exp.1:11:
He says that Peter, in Antioch, shared the table with the believers who were not Jews. But when some men came from James, he stopped doing so and drew away from them. The reason was fear of "those of the circumcision," that is, of the Jews who insisted that the others keep the law of Moses. "Drew back and separated" means that little by little he pulled apart from them.

Paul is the one speaking. He writes to the churches of Galatia and recounts this episode to defend that the gospel is the same for everyone. It is not known exactly what message those men from James brought, and it has been interpreted in several ways. What is clear is that Paul saw in Peter's conduct a contradiction with the truth of the gospel.

For today: the fear of what others think can lead us to treat our brothers and sisters differently. Let us ask for courage to welcome everyone as Christ welcomed us.
exp.1:13:
Paul tells how he saw that Peter and others were not acting in line with the truth of the gospel. So he spoke to Peter in front of everyone: if you, though you are a Jew, live like the Gentiles and not as a Jew does, why do you force the Gentiles to live as the Jews do? The word "compellest" means to force or pressure; to live as the Jews do means to follow the customs of the law.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. Peter used to eat with believers who were not Jews, but he pulled away from them out of fear when some men sent by James arrived. His example drew others along, even Barnabas. Paul corrected him because what was at stake was that salvation comes through faith in Christ.

Today: when, out of fear of what others think, we act differently from what we believe, we need to return to the gospel. Let us be consistent and welcome as equals all who trust in Christ.
exp.1:15:
This verse says that a person is not accepted before God by keeping the rules of the law of Moses, but by trusting in Jesus Christ. "Justified" means declared righteous, forgiven, and accepted by God. "No flesh" means no human being. Paul says that he and the other Jewish believers also put their trust in Christ for this very reason.

The apostle Paul is speaking. He has just told how he confronted Peter in front of everyone, because Peter was pulling away from the non-Jewish believers and so implied that they needed to follow Jewish customs to be fully accepted. Paul argues that the gospel is for everyone through faith. Some translate "faith of Christ" as "faith in Christ," and others as "faithfulness of Christ"; both ideas point to Jesus as the basis of our salvation.

Today we can rest from the pressure of earning God's love. We can obey him out of gratitude, not fear, because he has already accepted us through Christ.
exp.1:18:
It says that Paul, through the law, died to the law, so that he might live for God. The sentence about "á" being the old form of "a" must be removed, since it explains a word not in the verse. The idea is that the law itself brought him to a point where he could no longer live under its rule to be accepted by God, and so he was free to live for Him.

Paul writes to the Galatians, who were being pressured to add the works of the law to faith in Christ. Earlier, in Galatians 2, he has argued that we are justified by Christ. Here he explains his personal experience, and the next verse clarifies it: he is crucified with Christ. Interpreters explain in various ways how the law "put him to death," but all agree that he no longer depends on it to be righteous.

For today: do not spend your life trying to earn God's love by your performance. Rest in what Christ has done, and obey Him with gratitude.
exp.1:10:
Paul tells us that when Peter came to Antioch, he opposed him to his face, because Peter was wrong and deserved to be rebuked. "But" means "but," "I withstood him to the face" means that he confronted him directly, and "was to be blamed" means that he was at fault, that his conduct was worthy of reproach.

Paul writes to the Galatians to defend that the gospel is by grace, without adding the works of the law. He has just said that the leaders in Jerusalem accepted his mission. Now he shows that even Peter, so respected, was not exempt from correction. According to the following verses, Peter stopped eating with Gentile believers out of fear of the Jews, and others followed him.

For today: if we see that someone, even a beloved leader, acts against the gospel, we should speak to him with courage and respect, face to face and not behind his back. And we should also be willing to receive correction with humility.
exp.0:1:
This verse completes the letter's greeting. Paul writes to "the churches of Galatia" along with "all the brethren which are with me." The word "unto" is an old form of "to," and "brethren" refers to other believers who were with him. The verse does not say who they were or how many there were.

Paul is the one speaking, and he has just argued that his calling as an apostle comes from God and not from people. Galatia was a region, which is why he speaks of several churches rather than one. Scholars debate the exact location where these believers lived, but the letter makes clear that Paul writes with concern and firmness.

For today: the Christian faith is not lived alone. Paul does not write by himself but alongside other brothers. Seek a community of believers to walk with you, and pray for it.
exp.5:8:
It says that we should not grow weary of doing good, because in due season we will reap if we do not give up. "In due season" means "at the right moment." Reaping is harvesting, and the word translated as "weary" means worn out in strength or having given up.

The apostle Paul is speaking to the churches of Galatia. He has just explained that whatever a person sows, that they will reap: sowing for the flesh leads to ruin, and sowing for the Spirit leads to eternal life. With this in mind he encourages them to persevere, and then calls them to do good to everyone, especially to those of the household of faith.

For today: if you grow tired of helping, forgiving, or being steady in something good and you do not yet see results, do not give up. Choose one small good action, such as visiting someone or serving quietly, and keep at it, trusting that God takes care of the harvest.
exp.1:4:
Here Paul says that he did not yield, not even for an hour, to the false brothers. The phrase "we gave place by subjection" means that they did not submit or allow themselves to be pressured. His goal was that the truth of the gospel would remain firm among the Galatians, without mixing it with added requirements.

Paul writes in a letter to the churches of Galatia. He recounts what happened in Jerusalem, when some insisted that Titus, a Greek believer, be circumcised in order to be accepted. Paul saw in this an attempt to take away the freedom that is received in Christ, and so he stood firm.

For today: we can be kind to people, but we must not add rules or burdens to the message that we are saved by grace through faith in Christ. Let us ask God for wisdom to discern what is essential and what is not.
exp.4:6:
The explanation says that the believers in Galatia were doing very well in their Christian life, like a runner moving forward with strength. But someone hindered them, and Paul asks who stopped them so that they no longer obey the truth of the gospel.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. Some teachers were telling them that, besides believing in Christ, they had to keep the law, such as circumcision. Paul is concerned and speaks with firmness, but also with the pain of a pastor. He reminds them that what counts is the faith that works through love. Scholars debate exactly who those teachers were, but the central problem is clear.

For today: think about who or what has hindered your walk with God. It may be a teaching that adds burdens to the gospel, or a voice that takes away your freedom in Christ. Return to the simple truth: God receives you by faith, and that faith shows itself in love.
exp.3:7:
Paul says that before they knew God, the Galatians served "gods" that in reality are not gods. The idea of "serving" means they lived under their control, like slaves. "By nature" means those beings had no true divine nature; they were idols or false gods.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, mostly believers of non-Jewish origin. He reminds them of their past in paganism to show the contrast: they are now children of God. He is concerned that, under the influence of other teachers, they are returning to a life bound by rules and calendars, as if they needed that to please God.

For today: ask yourself what things you seek to feel secure or valued, such as success, the approval of others, or money. Remember that in Christ you are already a beloved child of God, and you do not have to serve anything that enslaves you.
exp.1:20:
Paul says that he does not reject or set aside the grace of God. Here, "reject" means to despise or push aside. Where the verse says "in vain," it means without purpose or without need. If a person could be declared righteous before God by keeping the law, then the death of Christ would have been pointless.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, where some taught that, in addition to believing in Christ, a person had to keep the law of Moses in order to be accepted by God. Just before this, Paul explained that his life now is lived by faith in the Son of God, who loved him and gave himself for him. That is why he argues that adding works to grace despises it.

For today: do not try to earn the love of God through your good behavior. Rest in what Christ has already done for you, and let that love move you to live thankful and obedient.
exp.3:21:
Paul recalls a fact found in Scripture: Abraham had two sons. One was born to a bondmaid, that is, a female slave (Hagar, who gave birth to Ishmael). The other was born to the freewoman (Sarah, mother of Isaac). The words "it is written" indicate that this comes from the Old Testament.

Paul is writing to Christians in Galatia who were drawn to living under the law of Moses in order to be accepted by God. He is concerned for them and asks whether they have really listened to what the law says. He uses the story of Abraham as an illustration, and in the verses that follow he explains it as an allegory, that is, a picture with a deeper meaning.

For today: you do not need to earn God's love through efforts and rules. Live as a free child, trusting in God's promise and in what Christ has done for you.
exp.0:20:
Paul says that, after his visit to Jerusalem, he went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia. These are areas north of Judea, in what would today be the southeast of Turkey and Syria.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia to defend that the gospel he preaches he received from Jesus Christ, not from men. For this reason he details his movements: he had almost no contact with the apostles in Jerusalem. In this way he shows that his message did not depend on them. Some believe that his hometown, Tarsus, was in Cilicia, but the text does not say so here.

God can shape a person in quiet, little-seen places, far from applause. If today you feel you are in a hidden or slow season, do not think that time is being wasted. Keep being faithful and learning from God, because He also works in the silent processes.
exp.4:20:
This verse ends the list of the "works of the flesh." Paul adds envyings, murders, drunkenness, and revelries (parties with excessive food and drink, where there is wild and uncontrolled behavior). Then he warns, as he had done before, that those who practice these things as a way of life will not inherit the kingdom of God. The word "I testify" here means "I solemnly declare."

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, which were confused and quarreling among themselves. He reminds them that Christian life is not lived by one's own effort or by the law, but guided by the Spirit. The verses that follow contrast these works with the fruit of the Spirit.

Today you might ask yourself: "What attitude dominates my life, such as envy or excess?" Bring it before God with sincerity and ask the Spirit to transform you. Cultivate love, peace, and self-control with God's help, not merely by willpower.
exp.3:24:
Paul says that Hagar, Abraham's servant, represents the covenant of the law given at Mount Sinai, in Arabia. The word "answereth" means "corresponds to" or "lines up with." So Hagar and Sinai are linked to the Jerusalem of Paul's time, which lived under the law, serving as a slave along with her children. The original text has some variations, and scholars interpret it in different ways.

Paul writes to the believers in Galatia, who were pressured to keep the law of Moses in order to be accepted by God. He uses the story of Abraham as an allegory: the son of the servant was born "after the flesh," and the son of the free woman was born through God's promise.

Today, do not live as someone who must earn God's love through effort and performance. In Christ you are a free son; obey with gratitude, not with fear.
exp.3:18:
Paul calls the believers in Galatia "my little children" and says that once again he feels the pains of childbirth for them. Those pains will continue until Christ is formed in them, that is, until his character and his way of life are truly seen in their lives. The word "until" marks the time when this will be complete, and "travail" speaks of suffering as a mother does when she gives birth.

Paul writes this letter with concern. Some teachers were telling them that, to be accepted by God, they had to add the law of Moses to faith in Christ. Paul, who had proclaimed the gospel to them, feels like an anxious mother as he sees them turning aside. His tone mixes tenderness and firmness.

For today: being a Christian is much more than keeping rules; it is letting Christ shape our hearts over time. We can pray for, and patiently and lovingly walk alongside, those who are growing in faith.
exp.3:22:
This verse says that Abraham had two sons by two different women. The son of the servant woman, Hagar, was born "according to the flesh," that is, through human effort and human planning. The son of the free woman, Sarah, was born "by promise," that is, because God had promised it and fulfilled it.

Paul is writing to the Christians of Galatia, who were being pressured to go back to depending on the law of Moses in order to be accepted by God. He uses the story of Abraham, Hagar, and Sarah as an illustration (he himself calls it an "allegory") to show the difference between trusting in one's own effort and trusting in God's promise.

For today: let us not try to earn God's favor through our achievements or through checklists of duties. Let us rest in what Christ has already done and in what God has promised, and live with gratitude rather than fear.
exp.3:12:
Paul reminds the Galatians that they know well how he first preached the gospel to them while he was ill or weak. "Infirmity of the flesh" speaks of a physical weakness; the word "infirmity" in the verse above captures that idea.

Paul writes with a warm, close tone to Christians who were drifting toward the law. He recalls the affection with which they received him at the beginning. We do not know with certainty what his illness was; some think of a problem with the eyes, based on verse 15, but that is only a possibility. He appeals to that relationship so that they will reflect.

For today: God can use our weakness to bless others. Do not wait until you are strong or perfect to share your faith; your sincere frailty can also show the grace of God.
exp.0:3:
It says that Jesus Christ gave himself, that is, gave his life, because of our sins. He did this to deliver us from this present evil world, meaning this age or this world marked by evil. And all of this was according to the will of God, whom Paul calls our Father.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia together with other brothers. In the greeting, he summarizes the gospel in one sentence. Soon, in verse 6, he will show his concern that some were turning away to a different gospel. That is why he reminds them from the start that salvation comes from what Christ did, not from what we manage to accomplish.

For today: when you feel pressured by the world or by guilt, remember that Jesus has already paid for your sins. Rest in his grace and live grateful, without trying to earn God's love.
exp.2:14:
Paul speaks to the brothers and sisters in Galatia and says he is going to use an example from everyday life: "I speak as a man." He explains that even a covenant or agreement between people, once it has been confirmed, no one sets aside or adds conditions to it. All the more, then, this cannot be done with what God has promised.

Paul was writing to Christians in Galatia who were being influenced to think they had to add works of the law in order to be accepted by God. For this reason he reminds them that the promise made to Abraham was already firmly established, and that the law came later and could not change it.

For today: you can rest in the fact that the salvation and promises of God depend on his faithfulness, not on your achievements. Trust in Christ, and do not add burdens that God did not place on you.
exp.0:5:
Paul says he is surprised, and troubled, that the Galatians have turned away so quickly from God, who called them through the grace of Christ, to follow a different gospel.

"Have ye been removed" means that they switched sides, like someone who deserts. "Grace" is God's favor, which cannot be earned.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. Unlike his usual pattern, he does not begin this letter with his customary thanksgiving, which shows his urgency. Some teachers were insisting that, in addition to believing in Christ, people had to keep certain requirements of the law in order to be accepted by God. Paul says that this is not another good news at all, but a distortion of the true one.

For today: examine what you have added to grace in your heart, such as feeling that you must earn God's love. Rest in what Christ has already done for you, and let that move you to obey him with gratitude.
exp.0:2:
Paul wishes the believers in Galatia to receive grace and peace. Grace is the undeserved favor of God, and peace is tranquility and reconciliation with Him. Both come together from two sources: God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ. The phrase about the old way of saying "with you" can be left out, since the reader sees "grace be to you" in the verse.

Paul writes this letter to several churches in Galatia. Before this greeting, he defends that his authority as an apostle comes from Jesus Christ and from God, not from men. This greeting is similar to the greetings in his other letters, but here it prepares the ground for correcting those who were turning away from the gospel.

For today: do not live trying to earn God's favor. Begin each day by remembering that His grace is already with you, and let that grace give you peace in the midst of your worries.
exp.0:15:
He says that God was pleased to reveal his Son "in me," that is, within Paul, so that he would proclaim Jesus among the non-Jews. After that, Paul did not immediately consult with ordinary human beings, the people around him in daily life. Words like "pleased" mean "was glad," and "consulted" means "sought counsel from."

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. Some were questioning his authority as an apostle and saying that his message came from men. That is why he tells his own story: Jesus himself called him, and he did not need others to give him permission or to teach him the gospel. The details of his travels appear in the verses that follow.

For today: When you sense that God is calling you to something, pray and seek his guidance in the Bible. Also ask for advice from wise believers, but remember that your security comes from Christ and not from the approval of people.
exp.4:4:
This verse says that believers, guided by the Holy Spirit, eagerly wait with confidence for the hope of being declared righteous before God, and that this comes through faith, not through our own efforts. "Wait" here means to await with certainty. "Righteousness" refers to being accepted as righteous before God.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. Some teachers were telling them that, to please God, they had to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses. Paul answers them firmly: whoever seeks to be made righteous by the law has fallen away from grace. Against that, he affirms that believers live differently: by the Spirit and by faith in Christ.

For today: do not live trying to earn God's favor with lists of merits. Rest in what Christ has done, and ask the Spirit to sustain you as you wait patiently and confidently for what God has promised.
exp.3:10:
Paul says that he is afraid for the Galatians. "I am afraid of you" means "I am concerned for you." He fears that all his effort in preaching to them, teaching them, and caring for them has been useless, that is, "in vain."

Paul writes to Christians in Galatia who came to know God through the gospel, but who were now returning to religious practices such as keeping days, months, and years, as if that would make them acceptable before God. Paul calls these practices "weak and beggarly elements": things that are weak and cannot save. He speaks with the pain of a father, not with coldness.

For today: if you notice that your faith is filling up with rules and outward appearances, return to what is essential: God knows you and loves you by grace in Christ. And if someone is drifting away, pray for that person and speak to them with kindness and truth.
exp.3:8:
Paul tells the Galatians that they already know God. Then he corrects himself: what matters even more is that God knows them and chose them. So he asks, sadly, why they would want to turn back to the weak and beggarly elements, that is, to basic teachings that are feeble and unable to save. "Turn back" means to return, and "weak" means without strength.

Paul wrote this letter to the churches of Galatia. Some teachers were telling them that, to please God, they had to keep the Jewish law, with its days and festivals. Paul reminds them that in Christ they are already children and heirs, not slaves. Interpreters debate exactly what these "elements" were, but all agree that they were human or religious rules that enslave.

Today we might ask ourselves whether we trust our religious practices to earn God's love. Rest in this: God already knows you and has received you as his child through Christ.
exp.2:24:
What it says: Paul explains that, now that faith in Christ has come, we are no longer under a schoolmaster. In that time, the schoolmaster was a guide or tutor, often a trusted slave, who looked after and disciplined the child until he grew up. Here the schoolmaster is the law.

Context: Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, where some wanted to return to keeping the law of Moses in order to be accepted by God. He answers that the law had a temporary role: to lead us to Christ. Now, through faith, all of us are children of God.

For today: Do not live trying to earn God's love through lists of rules or achievements. Rules can guide you, but your identity rests in Christ. Obey as a beloved child, not as someone who fears being rejected.
exp.1:2:
It says that Titus, Paul's companion, was a Greek, meaning he was not Jewish, and yet no one forced him to be circumcised. Circumcision was the sign of the law of Moses for Jewish men.

Paul speaks here in his letter to the Galatians. He tells of his visit to Jerusalem with Barnabas and Titus, to set out the gospel before the leaders. Titus was a living example: a believer who was not Jewish and was accepted without being required to be circumcised. Paul argues that salvation is by grace, not by adding requirements from the law. Some commentators debate whether Titus was or was not pressured; the text says he was not compelled.

For today: let us not add human rules to the grace of Christ. Let us welcome others because of their faith in Jesus, without demanding extra requirements before they feel accepted.
exp.5:14:
For those united with Christ, outward religious marks are not what matters most. Being circumcised or not does not change our standing before God. What counts is the new creation, that is, a new life that God himself produces in the person.

Paul writes to the Galatians, who were being pressured by some to be circumcised in order to be accepted by God. Paul replies that we should not boast in rituals, but only in the cross of Christ. Through it, their old way of living and of valuing things comes to an end.

For today: do not measure your faith by customs, titles, or religious appearances. Ask God to keep renewing your heart and your way of treating others.
exp.4:0:
It says that we should stay firm in the freedom that Christ gave us. Paul asks us not to go back under that burden.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. Some teachers were telling them that, besides believing in Christ, they had to keep the law of Moses, above all circumcision, in order to be accepted by God. Paul replies that trusting in that takes away the value of Christ's work. The verses that follow make this clear.

Today we can fall into thinking that God accepts us because of our works, rules, or efforts. This week, when you feel guilt or pressure to earn God's love, remember that Christ has already made you free. Rest in his grace and obey out of love, not out of fear.
exp.0:11:
Paul says that the gospel he preaches was not handed to him by any human being, nor did he learn it in a school or from other teachers. He received it directly "by the revelation of Jesus Christ," that is, because Jesus himself made it known to him. The word "revelation" means that God uncovers something that could not be seen before.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, where some teachers were saying that his message was secondhand and needed correcting. He insists that his message of salvation by grace does not come from human opinions. He then recalls his former life as a persecutor, to show that his change can be explained only by God's action. Scholars debate when and how this revelation happened, but Paul ties it to his encounter with Christ.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our faith rests on customs, popular opinions, or on Jesus himself. Let us read the Gospels with humility and ask God to teach us to know him truly.
exp.5:0:
If a fellow believer is caught doing something wrong, the text says that those who live guided by the Spirit should help him get back up, treating him kindly and with humility.
