"Caught" means found out or trapped in an error. "Restore" is like putting back in its proper place something that has been broken. "Gentleness" means kindness. And "tempted" means tested or put to the trial. It also warns each person to watch over himself, because he too could fall.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, writing to the churches of Galatia. He teaches them to live in freedom through the Spirit, without fighting among themselves. The verses that follow speak of carrying one another's burdens and of not thinking oneself superior.

Today, if someone close to you stumbles, do not judge or expose him. Speak to him in private, with affection and patience, remembering that you too need grace.
exp.1:17:
He says that if someone rebuilds what they once tore down, they show themselves to be guilty. A word that appears in the source wording for a person who breaks a rule is not used here, so I have simply described that person in plain terms: someone who breaks a rule. The verb meaning to put back up something that had been knocked down is expressed in the verse as "build again," so the explanation of it is rendered with that wording.

Paul writes to the Galatians, who were being pressed to add the law of Moses to faith in Christ. Earlier he had explained in Antioch that people are made right with God through faith, not through works of the law. Here he speaks in the first person as an example. Interpreters debate exactly what was "torn down," but the general sense is that he had given up the law as a way to be accepted by God. Going back to it would contradict himself.

For today: do not return to trying to earn God's love through your good behavior. Obey out of gratitude, resting in what Christ has already done for you.
exp.2:25:
This verse says that all believers are children of God, not because they keep the law or because they belong to a people, but because they trust in Christ Jesus. A guide or tutor is someone who looked after children until they grew up.

Paul writes to the Christians of Galatia. Some were teaching them that, to be fully part of God's people, they had to follow the law of Moses. Paul answers that the law was like a guardian who prepared the way toward Christ. Now that faith has come, everyone, Jews and non-Jews alike, enters God's family in the same way.

For today: you do not have to earn God's love through effort or compare yourself with others. If you trust in Christ, you are already a son or daughter of God. Live with that assurance, and treat other believers as brothers and sisters, regardless of their background or condition.
exp.0:8:
As Paul said before, he now says again with firmness: if anyone preaches to you a gospel other than the one you have received, let that person be accursed. The word "accursed" means cursed, set apart, and given over to God's judgment. The phrase "a gospel other than the one you received" means a message different from the message of Christ.

Paul is writing to the churches of Galatia. Some people were troubling them and wanted to change the message of grace, probably by adding requirements for being saved. Paul repeats the warning so that no one takes it lightly, and he makes clear that his authority does not depend on pleasing people.

For today: compare what you hear, even when it comes from someone respected or persuasive, with what the Scriptures say about Jesus. If it adds conditions to the grace of Christ, be careful and return to the Bible.
exp.4:16:
The explanation says that within the believer there is a struggle. The "flesh" is our human nature inclined toward selfishness and sin, and "lust" means it strongly desires. The Spirit desires the opposite. The two are opposed, so we cannot always do what we would want, that is, whatever we desire.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, who were quarreling among themselves and arguing about the law. He tells them to live led by the Spirit, not by the impulses of the flesh. Some interpret the last part as describing the believer's frustration; others, that the Spirit keeps the flesh from getting its way. Both readings are possible.

Today, when you feel the urge to respond with anger or selfishness, pause and pray. Ask the Spirit to guide you to choose love.
exp.5:16:
He says that from now on no one should cause him trouble or bother him, because Paul carries in his body the "marks" of Jesus. The word "marks" (in Greek, stigmata) referred to signs or scars, like the brands that masters placed on their slaves.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, where some wanted to make circumcision a requirement for being accepted by God. He had already suffered beatings and persecution for preaching Christ (Acts 14:19; 2 Corinthians 11:23-25). Many believe he is referring to those scars, although the Bible does not spell this out. With this he closes the discussion: his life already shows whom he belongs to.

For today: what proves our faith is not arguments or religious appearances, but a life given to Christ, even when it costs. Live in such a way that others can see whom you belong to.
exp.4:9:
Paul says that he trusts the Galatians, united with the Lord, will not end up thinking differently from what he taught them. He also warns that whoever is troubling or confusing them will bear God's judgment, whoever that person may be. Here "troubling" means disturbing or confusing, and "think" means to suppose or be of the opinion that something is so.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, who were being influenced by teachers who added circumcision and the law as a requirement for being saved. He corrects them firmly, but he shows confidence in them. He does not name the person who was troubling them; he says "whoever that person may be." This reminds us that his confidence rested in the Lord, not in themselves.

For today: when someone confuses you with teachings that add requirements to the gospel of grace, return to Scripture and trust that God sustains his own.
exp.5:5:
The explanation says that the one who receives teaching from God's Word should share with his teacher "in all good things." "Communicate" is an old word meaning to share or to give a part. "Good things" can include money, food, lodging and other material help, though some also think of broader support such as affection and cooperation.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. Shortly before, he spoke of bearing one another's burdens and of each person examining his own work. Here he gives a concrete example of generosity. What follows, about sowing and reaping, suggests that giving is a sowing that God sees and rewards.

Today, we can support those who teach us the Bible with generosity and gratitude, whether through offerings, practical help or words of encouragement, without taking their work for granted.
exp.1:12:
The explanation says that the other Jewish believers in Antioch also acted hypocritically along with Peter. The words "dissembled" and "dissimulation" mean pretending to think one way while actually thinking another, or acting out of fear. Even Barnabas, a very dear companion of Paul, was swept along by that attitude.

The speaker is Paul, who tells the Galatians what happened in Antioch. Peter had been eating with non-Jewish believers, but he withdrew when some men came from James, out of fear of what they would think. Paul confronted him because that conduct contradicted the gospel: faith in Christ unites everyone at one table.

Today, we might ask ourselves whether we change our behavior depending on who is watching us. Good examples and bad ones are contagious. Let us ask God for the courage to live with consistency and to accept correction with humility.
exp.2:17:
Paul says that God's inheritance cannot come by two paths at the same time. If it were received by keeping the law, it would no longer be a promise. But God gave it to Abraham as a gift, through a promise. The explanation's notes on the words "donation" and "inheritance" and "however" are not needed here, since those words do not appear in the verse you are reading.

Paul writes to the Christians of Galatia, who were being pressured to depend on the law of Moses to be accepted by God. He had already explained that the promise came first, and that the law arrived 430 years later. For that reason, the law could not cancel what God had already promised.

For today: you do not have to earn God's love through religious effort. Receive his gift in Christ with gratitude, and let that gratitude move your obedience, not fear.
exp.2:13:
He says that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law for a double purpose: so that the blessing promised to Abraham would also come to the non-Jews (the "Gentiles"), and so that all of us, through faith, would receive the promised Holy Spirit.

The apostle Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. Some wanted the believers who were not Jewish to keep the law of Moses in order to be accepted by God. Paul answers that the blessing never came through obeying the law, but through faith, just as it did with Abraham. Christ bore the curse so that this path would be open to us.

For today: you do not have to earn God's love by your efforts or by your background. Trust in Christ, and rest in the knowledge that God's Spirit is a gift received by faith, not a reward for behaving well.
exp.1:19:
He says that Paul considers himself united with Christ in his death: his old way of living, centered on himself, was crucified. Now Christ lives in him. The word "together" is rendered here as "with," and "in the flesh" refers to his daily life in this body. Paul lives by trusting the Son of God, who loved him and gave himself for him.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, where some were teaching that the law of Moses had to be kept in order to be made right with God. He answers that the law does not save, and that the new life is born from faith in Christ. For that reason he adds that he does not set aside the grace of God.

Today, when facing a decision or a burden, we can ask ourselves: "Am I acting out of pride or fear, or trusting in the love of Christ?" Bringing that moment to God in prayer helps us live supported by his grace, not by our own effort.
exp.2:1:
Paul asks the Galatians a simple question: how did you receive the Holy Spirit? Was it by keeping the law of Moses, or by hearing the message of the gospel and believing it? Where the explanation refers to "you" as a plural, it means you all, and "hearing with faith" refers to listening to the message of Christ with faith.

Paul writes firmly to the churches of Galatia. Some teachers were telling them that, in addition to believing in Jesus, they had to keep the law in order to be accepted by God. Paul reminds them of their own experience: they had already received the Spirit when they believed, without doing works of the law. His question aims to get them to recognize what God had already done.

For today: do not spend your life trying to earn God's love through your own efforts. Trust in Christ every day, and let his Spirit transform you.
exp.1:14:
Paul says: "We are Jews by birth, not sinners from among the Gentiles." The phrase "by birth" means Jews by nature, not those who became Jews later through conversion. The expression "sinners of the Gentiles" was a common way among Jews of speaking about non-Jews, whom they regarded as outside the law of God.

Paul speaks to Peter in Antioch, in front of everyone. Peter had stopped eating with Gentile believers out of fear of other Jews. Paul begins here with what both of them shared as Jews, and right away shows that they too were justified not by the law, but by faith in Christ.

For today: no background, tradition, or good record makes us right before God. If Christ received us by pure grace, let us treat others with that same acceptance, without making anyone feel inferior.
exp.2:20:
Paul asks whether the law of Moses is opposed to the promises God made to Abraham. He answers firmly: "God forbid!" He explains that if the law had been able to give life (to give life means to make alive), then righteousness, that is, being accepted by God, would have been gained by obeying it.

Paul writes to the Galatians, believers who were being pressured to add the law to faith in Christ. He makes clear to them that the law and the promise are not in competition: the law showed sin, but it could not save. Only the promise, received by faith, gives life.

For today: let us not trust in our good works to earn God's favor. Obeying him is good, but our security rests in Jesus Christ. Rest in his grace and obey with gratitude.
exp.4:3:
It says that those who try to be declared righteous before God through the law are left "empty of Christ," meaning cut off from Him and without receiving His benefit. "You are trying to be justified" means seeking to be accepted by God. "You have fallen" from grace means they left the path of God's undeserved favor to rely on their own efforts.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. Some teachers were insisting that non-Jewish believers had to be circumcised and keep the law in order to be saved. Paul answers firmly: adding the law to Christ denies that Christ is enough. He then points out that hope lies in faith that works through love.

For today: do not try to earn God's favor through good works, religiousness, or perfection. Rest in Christ, and let your obedience come from love and gratitude.
exp.2:7:
This verse says that Scripture, looking ahead, already knew that God would make non-Jewish people right with him through faith. So God announced the good news to Abraham in advance, promising him: "In you all nations will be blessed." The word "preached" means that it announced the good news, and "justify" means to declare someone righteous.

Paul writes to the Galatians, believers who were being pressured to add the works of the law of Moses to their faith in Christ. To answer them, Paul reminds them of Abraham, who was accepted by God because he believed, long before the law existed. In this way he shows that God's plan has always included all peoples.

For today: no one has to earn God's favor through effort or merit. Trust God as Abraham did, and welcome others with joy, regardless of their background, because the promise is for everyone.
exp.2:10:
The explanation says that no one is made righteous before God by keeping the law. "Being justified" means being accepted and counted clean before Him. Paul proves this with a line of Scripture: "the just shall live by faith." In other words, true life with God comes through trusting Him, not through straining to keep rules.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, where some taught that, in order to please God, the law of Moses had to be added to faith in Christ. He answers that the law demanded perfect obedience in everything, and so it condemned anyone who did not achieve it. He cites Habakkuk 2:4 to show that faith has always been the way. Then he explains that Christ bore that curse for us.

Today, you do not have to earn God's love by your good behavior. Trust in Christ, rest in His forgiveness, and obey out of gratitude, not out of fear.
exp.4:10:
Paul tells the Galatians: "Brothers, if I still preached that people must be circumcised, why are they still persecuting me?" If he did that, he says, the "offence of the cross" would have ceased. "Offence" means a stumbling block, something that gives offense. "Suffer persecution" means to endure hardship.

Paul writes to churches in Galatia, where some teachers taught that believers had to be circumcised in order to be saved. Some think these teachers accused Paul of preaching this in other places. He answers that his suffering proves the opposite: he preached that salvation is by grace alone, through the cross, and that message offended many.

For today: the message of the cross does not depend on our merits, and at times it is uncomfortable. Let us ask for courage to proclaim it with love, without adding human requirements to make it more acceptable.
exp.5:15:
Paul wishes peace and mercy on everyone who lives by this rule. This rule is what he has just said: what matters is not circumcision, but being a new creation in Christ. The source words here are not for your reader to see, so I will simply describe the idea: to live or walk in a certain way. Mercy is God's compassion toward us.

Paul writes this letter to the churches of Galatia, where some teachers insisted that believers had to be circumcised and follow the law of Moses in order to be accepted by God. As he closes the letter, Paul sums up his message: only the cross of Christ makes us new. The phrase "the Israel of God" is understood in different ways: many believe it refers to all believers, both Jews and Gentiles; others think it points to Jewish believers in particular.

Today, instead of measuring ourselves by outward rules or by comparisons, we can live each day trusting in what Christ did on the cross, and so receive his peace and his mercy.
exp.3:1:
He says that a child who is heir, although he is owner of everything, lives under the care of guardians (those who lead and watch over him) and managers (those who administer his property). This lasts until the date his father has already set. In the meantime, he is like a servant, because he does not command or decide.

Paul writes to the Galatians, who were tempted to return to the law as a way to please God. He uses a scene common in his time to show that the law had a temporary role, until God sent his Son. Scholars debate details of the legal customs Paul had in mind, but the central idea is clear.

For today: if you are a child of God through Christ, do not live with the fear of a servant. Trust that God knows the times of your growing, and walk with the freedom and responsibility of a son.
exp.2:5:
It says that Abraham trusted God, and that God counted that trust as righteousness. To believe means that he relied on what God had promised him. The phrase "accounted to him" is an older way of saying that God credited it to him, or regarded him as being in the right. Here, righteousness means being right before God. The verse quotes Genesis 15:6.

The apostle Paul writes to Christians in Galatia. Some were pressing them to depend on keeping the law in order to please God. Paul reminds them that they received the Spirit and saw powerful works when they heard with faith, not by keeping rules. He sets Abraham as an example: before the law, God accepted him because he believed God.

For today: you do not have to earn God's love through good behavior. Trust in Him and in what Christ has done, and from there live thankfully, obeying out of love and not out of fear or to impress anyone.
exp.3:3:
When the appointed time had fully come, God sent forth his Son. Jesus was born of a woman, that is, he was truly human, and he lived under the law of Moses. "Under the law" means that he was under its authority. "Fullness of time" refers to the set time, arrived at its full measure.

The apostle Paul writes to the Galatians, who were turning back to depend on the law to be accepted by God. Earlier he compared a child heir, who lives under guardians until the date his father has set. Paul shows that the coming of Christ marks the move from that stage to the freedom of the children of God.

For today: you do not have to earn God's love through religious effort. Christ came for you, so you can approach God with confidence, as a child to his father. And when life seems slow or confusing, remember that God knows when to act.
exp.5:9:
As long as we have the opportunity, the verse says, we should do good to all people, and especially to those who belong to the household of faith, meaning the other believers who are members of God's family.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, who were being pressured to return to the law. Just before this, he encouraged them not to grow weary of doing good, because there will be a harvest in due time. This verse applies that idea: the Christian life shows itself in concrete acts of love, first within the church and also toward everyone.

Today you can choose a specific person, from your church or your surroundings, and help them this week with something simple: a visit, a meal, a phone call, or a favor. Do it without expecting anything in return.
exp.1:16:
It says that if, while seeking to be declared righteous before God through Christ, we ourselves, even we Jews, are found to be sinners (like the Gentiles), that does not make Christ a servant or promoter of sin. Paul answers firmly: "God forbid," that is, never! "Declared righteous" means being counted as righteous before God.

Paul is speaking to the Galatians and recalls what he said to Peter in Antioch. Some thought that leaving the law as a way to salvation led to living in sin. Scholars explain the exact meaning of "found to be sinners" in several ways, but Paul rejects the idea that Christ encourages sin.

For today: grace is not an excuse to sin. Trust in Christ to be righteous before God, and let that faith lead you to live in a way that pleases him.
exp.4:11:
Paul says he wishes that those who unsettle the Galatians would even cut themselves off. To unsettle means to disturb and confuse. "Cut off" can be understood in two ways: separated from the community, or mutilated, meaning that they would castrate themselves. Many scholars prefer this second reading, but there is no full agreement.

Paul writes in anger to churches confused by teachers who demanded circumcision for salvation. With very strong irony, he says that if they are so set on cutting the flesh, they should go all the way. For him, this denied the cross, where Christ had already done everything.

Today, we should not use this tone as a model for treating others. But we can learn to firmly defend the gospel of grace when someone adds requirements to what Christ has already done, and to do so with love.
exp.2:27:
It says that, for God, the differences that divide people are not what decides who belongs to his family. Where the text says "bond," that means a slave; "free" means a free person; and "male" means a man, while "female" means a woman. "Ye are all one" means "you are all one." Believers form one family in Christ.

Paul writes to the churches in Galatia, where some were teaching that non-Jewish believers had to follow the law of Moses in order to be accepted. Paul answers that faith in Christ, not one's background or the law, makes us children of God and heirs of the promise made to Abraham. The verses before this one speak of baptism as being "clothed with Christ."

For today: in the church and in everyday life, treat each person as a brother or sister in Christ, regardless of nationality, social class, or gender. This week, look for ways to reach out to someone who is different from you.
exp.1:6:
They said that the leaders in Jerusalem recognized that God had entrusted Paul with proclaiming the gospel to those who were not Jews (the "uncircumcised"), just as he had entrusted Peter with it for the Jews (the "circumcised"). "But on the contrary" means "on the contrary." "When they saw" means "when they saw."

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia to defend that the gospel comes by grace, without adding the law of Moses to it. Here he tells how Peter, James, and John did not impose anything more on him, but recognized his calling. In this way he shows that his message was the same as theirs.

For today: God calls different people to serve in different ways. Instead of comparing ourselves or competing, we can recognize and support the work of other believers, while all of us stand firm in the same gospel of Christ.
exp.2:23:
The explanation says that the law of Moses was like a "schoolmaster," an old word for the guide or tutor who looked after and disciplined a child until he grew up. Its purpose was to bring us to Christ, so that God would declare us righteous by faith, not by keeping rules.

Paul writes to the believers in Galatia, who were being pressured to add Jewish law to their faith in Jesus. He explains that the law had a temporary purpose: to show sin and point to the need for a Savior. Some understand "schoolmaster" as a protector, others as a disciplinarian; both ideas fit.

For today: do not rely on your good behavior to be accepted by God. Let the awareness of your failings draw you closer to Christ, and live thankfully, resting in his grace.
exp.5:10:
Paul tells the Galatians to notice the size of the letters he is writing to them, a thing done "with mine own hand." "Ye see" means "look" or "notice." Up to this point, another person may have written the letter, and now Paul takes the pen himself.

Paul speaks to the churches of Galatia, who were being pressed to be circumcised in order to be accepted by God. At the end of the letter, he writes in his own hand to give weight to his words. Scholars debate why the letters were large: some think it was for emphasis, others that he had poor eyesight, but the Bible does not make it clear.

Today, when something is very important, it is worth saying it clearly and sincerely, without beating around the bush. And we can also listen closely to what is essential: that Christ is enough, and that doing good springs from that faith.
exp.0:17:
Paul says that three years after the events in Damascus and Arabia, he went up to Jerusalem to get to know Peter, and he stayed with him for fifteen days.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia to defend the claim that the gospel he preaches came directly from Christ, not from human leaders. That is why he details his movements: he did not rush to seek the approval of the apostles. The three years are counted either from his conversion or from his return to Damascus; commentators do not agree on which. What is not stated is what they talked about during those fifteen days.

For today: value the counsel and fellowship of mature believers, but let your faith rest on Christ himself. Learn from others with humility, without depending on them to believe.
exp.4:1:
What it says: Paul speaks with great seriousness. "Behold" is like saying "pay close attention." When the explanation says "if ye be circumcised" means "if you let yourselves be circumcised," and "Christ shall profit you nothing" means "Christ will be of no use to you," the point is this: if they trust in circumcision to be accepted by God, Christ no longer benefits them.

Context: Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. Some teachers were teaching that, to be saved, non-Jewish believers had to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses. Paul defends that salvation is by grace, not by adding works to Christ.

For today: Examine whether you are trusting in your efforts, rituals, or good behavior to earn God's favor. Rest in Christ, who has already done what was necessary, and obey God as a response of love, not as payment.
exp.2:22:
Here Paul says that, before faith in Christ arrived, the Jews lived under the law as if under guard and shut in, as if under watch. The explanation of the word for "but" and the word for "revealed" is unnecessary here, so I have left those out. The law protected and restricted people while the coming of Christ was being prepared.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, where some were teaching that people had to keep the law of Moses in order to be righteous before God. He answers that the law is not against God's promises, but it cannot give life. Its task was to show sin and point toward Christ, like a guardian, that is, a guide who looks after a child until he grows up.

Today we can be thankful that God accepts us because we trust in Jesus, not because we keep a list of rules. Rules can guide us, but only Christ gives us life and freedom.
exp.0:7:
If anyone, even Paul and his companions or an angel from heaven, were to preach a gospel different from the one the Galatians had already received, that person would be "accursed." This older word means cursed, set apart, and handed over to God's judgment. The verse's "preach" and "preached" are the same word in the explanation's wording, so "preach" fits here, and "have preached unto you" matches what the Galatians had already heard.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. He is surprised that they are turning away so quickly from the grace of Christ, since some were troubling them and wanted to twist the message. Paul includes himself to show that authority does not rest in the person but in the gospel that was received. His words are very strong, but his concern is that the truth of salvation by grace not be lost.

Today, before accepting any teaching, however attractive or respected the person who gives it may be, compare it with what Christ and the apostles taught in the Bible. Follow the truth, not popularity.
exp.1:7:
This verse says that God, who gave power to Peter for his work among the Jews (the circumcision), also gave power to Paul for his work among the non-Jews (the Gentiles). The phrase "wrought effectually in" means God was at work in both of them.

Paul speaks to the Galatians and tells what happened when he met with the leaders in Jerusalem. Some were saying that his message was inferior or needed correction. Paul maintains that his calling did not come from men but from God, and that the leading apostles recognized it when they saw the fruits of his ministry.

For today: God calls different people to serve in different ways. Instead of comparing ourselves with others or belittling their service, we can recognize God's work in them and work together with humility in what He has entrusted to us.
exp.2:21:
The Scripture declared all people to be held prisoners under sin, meaning it shut them in as captives with no way out through their own effort. The purpose was that the promise of God would be given to those who believe, and this through faith in Jesus Christ. Where the explanation notes older spellings, the verse's "hath concluded" is simply the older way of saying the Scripture has shut all people in under sin.

Paul writes to the Galatians, who were being tempted to add the law of Moses to faith in Christ. He asks whether the law is against God's promises, and he answers that it is not. But the law could never give life; its role was to show that all of us need a Savior. The promise to Abraham is received by faith.

Today you can rest in the knowledge that your relationship with God does not depend on your good performance. Acknowledge your failures with humility and trust in Christ. That faith frees you from living in fear or from comparing yourself with others.
exp.4:15:
Paul says that we should live guided by the Holy Spirit, and not give in to the wrong desires of our human nature. The verse's command to "walk" means to live day by day in the Spirit. The wrong desires he describes are strong longings for what is wrong. "Flesh" here does not mean the body, but our tendency to live for self and far from God.

Paul writes to the churches in Galatia. There were quarrels among them, and some wanted to go back to depending on the law to be accepted. He reminds them that love for one's neighbor sums up the law, and that biting and fighting destroy them. His answer is not more rules, but depending on the Spirit.

For today: when you feel anger, envy, or the urge to hurt someone, stop and pray: "Holy Spirit, guide me now." Then choose an act of love, such as answering calmly or asking forgiveness.
exp.1:8:
Paul tells how James, Cephas (Peter) and John, who were regarded as "pillars" of the church, recognized the grace God had given him. So they gave their right hands to him and to Barnabas as a sign of fellowship and agreement. Thus Paul and Barnabas would go to the Gentiles (the non-Jews), and they would go to those of the circumcision (the Jews).

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia and defends that his message comes from God. He tells that the leaders in Jerusalem added nothing to the gospel, but approved his calling. This shows unity in what is essential, even though each one had a different field of work.

For today: value other believers who serve differently from you. There is no need to compete. If God has called them and their fruit is evident, give them your hand and work together for the same gospel.
exp.5:4:
This verse says that each person will have to answer for their own life and their own responsibilities. The word "burden" here refers to the personal weight of our actions, and "shall bear" means that each one will carry it himself.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians of Galatia. A few verses earlier he asked them to help one another with heavy burdens (6:2). Now he makes clear that, even so, no one can hide behind others or compare themselves with them to feel better. Each person must examine his own work before God. Scholars note that in the original language there are two different words for "burden": one is a huge weight that needs help, and the other is personal responsibility.

Today we can help those who suffer, but without failing to carry our own load. Instead of comparing yourself with others or blaming them, ask yourself honestly: "What is mine to do today before God?"
exp.2:15:
This verse says that God made promises to Abraham and to his offspring, that is, to his descendants. Paul points out that the word is in the singular, not the plural, as if speaking of one person, and he affirms that this offspring is Christ. The word "seed" in the verse means offspring or descendant; "were made" is the verse's own wording, and it means the promises were given.

Paul writes to the believers in Galatia, who were being influenced to think they had to keep the law in order to be accepted by God. He reminds them that the promise came first, and that a covenant once confirmed is not changed. His argument follows the way he understood the text of Genesis; some scholars see it as a reading of Christ as the head of a people, not only as an individual.

For today: your relationship with God rests on what Christ did, not on your performance. Rest in his promise and respond with gratitude.
exp.1:3:
It says there were "false brothers," people who claimed to be believers but were not truly so. They slipped in "secretly," like spies, to watch the freedom we have through Christ. Their aim was "to bring us into bondage," that is, to make us slaves to religious rules. Here "spy out" means to watch with bad intent.

Paul is speaking, writing to the Galatians. He has just told how in Jerusalem Titus, who was a Greek, was not forced to be circumcised. Paul explains that some wanted to impose circumcision as a requirement for being saved. Many understand this to refer to certain Judaizers, but the text gives no further details. Paul did not give in, in order to protect the truth of the gospel.

Today, let us not allow anyone to load us with requirements that God did not ask for in order to be accepted by Him. Let us examine what we hear with the Bible in hand, and defend with humility the freedom that Christ gave us.
exp.3:16:
They show great interest and affection for the Galatians, but with bad motives. The phrase "they zealously affect you" means they seek them out eagerly. "Exclude" means to shut them out, to leave them on the outside. Their aim is that the Galatians will then seek them out and admire them.

The apostle Paul is speaking to the churches of Galatia. Some teachers were pressing them to add the law as a requirement for being saved. Paul fears they will be cut off from the freedom of the gospel. Interpreters disagree about exactly who they were, but the context points to those teachers.

For today: do not confuse attention with true love. Ask yourself whether the person who encourages you to follow them brings you closer to Christ or only to their own influence. A good guide leads you to Jesus, not to depending on them.
exp.0:18:
In that visit to Jerusalem, Paul saw none of the other apostles, only James, whom he calls "the Lord's brother." The word "but" means "except," and "saw" and "went" are older ways of speaking. "The Lord's brother" is understood in different ways: many believe he was a brother of Jesus through Mary, while others see him as a close relative.

Paul writes in his letter to the Galatians. Some doubted his authority and thought his message came from the apostles in Jerusalem. He makes clear that he received the gospel directly from Jesus Christ, and that his contact with the other leaders was brief and limited. That is why he adds, almost like an oath, that he is not lying.

For today: let us be honest and clear about how we have come to believe what we believe. Let us gratefully acknowledge those whom God used along our way, but let us place our faith in Christ himself, and not only in people.
exp.4:7:
What it says: Paul states that the way of thinking that pulled the Galatians away from the truth does not come from God, who is the one who calls them. The word "persuasion" in the verse refers to the conviction or influence that makes you change your mind. "The one who calls you" refers to God.

Context: Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, who were listening to teachers saying that, in addition to believing in Christ, they had to be circumcised and keep the law to be accepted. Paul, with the tone of a worried pastor, reminds them that they started well and asks who stopped them. His answer is clear: that teaching did not come from God.

For today: When a teaching pulls you away from grace and from faith that works through love, test it against the Bible and ask yourself whether it truly comes from God. Not every convincing voice is the voice of the one who called you.
exp.3:19:
Paul says he wishes he could be with the Galatians right now and change his tone of voice. "Change my voice" means speaking to them in a different way, perhaps with more tenderness. "Stand in doubt of you" means being confused, not knowing what to think about them. "I desire to be present with you now" is the same as saying he truly wishes he were there.

Paul writes to them like a worried father. The Galatians were giving up the freedom of the gospel to go back to depending on the law as a way of salvation. He calls them "my little children" and suffers for them as in childbirth. Through a letter he cannot see their faces or gauge their reactions, and so he feels limited. Some scholars think he wanted to soften his tone; others, that he wanted to speak to them with more firmness. The text does not make this clear.

For today: when someone you love goes astray, do not stay silent or treat them coldly. Speak with truth, but with the heart of a father or mother, asking God for wisdom to find the right tone.
exp.5:6:
It says that no one should be deceived: God cannot be mocked or treated lightly. Whatever a person sows with their life, that same thing they will harvest. "Reap" means to gather the harvest, and "cannot be mocked" means that no one can escape his justice by pretending not to notice.

Paul writes to the believers in Galatia. Just before this, he speaks of helping one another and of sharing with those who teach the Word. With this warning, he reminds them that their choices and their generosity have consequences. What follows shows two paths: sowing for the flesh, which leads to corruption, or sowing for the Spirit, which leads to eternal life.

For today: think about what you are sowing with your time, your money, and your words. Today you can sow something good, such as supporting someone, forgiving, or giving a moment to prayer, and trust that God will make the fruit grow in its time.
exp.2:0:
Paul says to the Galatians: "How foolish you are! Who has put a spell on you, so that you no longer obey the truth?" He reminds them that Jesus Christ was clearly presented to them as crucified among them. The word "foolish" means without understanding, and "bewitched" means put a spell on or deceived.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, concerned that some teachers were telling them that, in addition to believing in Christ, they had to keep the law of Moses to be accepted by God. He speaks with firmness, but with the pain of a pastor who loves his people. Scholars debate exactly where these churches were, but the central message is clear.

For today: when you feel tempted to earn God's love through effort and rules, look again at the cross. There Christ did what you could not do.
exp.4:2:
Paul says that he gives a solemn testimony, once again, to every man who decides to be circumcised. Here "to protest" means to declare with seriousness, not to complain. The warning is clear: whoever gets circumcised in order to be accepted by God becomes obligated to keep the whole law of Moses, not just part of it.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. Some teachers were telling them that, to be fully part of God's people, non-Jewish believers had to be circumcised and keep the law. Paul answers that this changes where their trust lies: instead of resting on Christ, it becomes their own effort. It would be going back to a yoke that no one can carry completely.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are adding rules or achievements to feel accepted by God. Rest in what Christ has done for you. From that freedom, serve others with love and gratitude, not with fear or in order to earn approval.
exp.4:22:
This verse closes the list of the fruit of the Spirit with two qualities: meekness and temperance. Meekness is strength under control, a gentle character that does not seek to dominate. Temperance is self-control, knowing how to say no to disordered impulses. Then Paul adds that against such things there is no law: no one could condemn a life like this.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, who felt pressured to live under the law of Moses. He shows them that the Spirit produces in the believer a character that the law aimed for but could not give. Earlier he had mentioned the works of the flesh, and now he presents the contrast.

For today: when you become angry or are tempted toward excess, before reacting, pause and ask the Spirit for calm and self-control. It is a fruit that God grows over time, not something you achieve by willpower alone.
exp.4:18:
Paul says that the works of the flesh are plain to see. He names four here: adultery (unfaithfulness in marriage), fornication (sex outside of marriage), uncleanness (impurity, a dirty or impure way of living), and lasciviousness (living without restraint or control, given over to pleasure).

The word "flesh" here does not mean the body, but our human nature leaning toward sin.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. He teaches them that following Christ does not mean returning to the law as a way to be saved, but it also does not mean living without limits. Earlier he explained that the flesh and the Spirit struggle against each other, and that whoever is guided by the Spirit lives differently.

For today: it is not enough to say "I don't want to sin." Each day, ask God to guide you by his Spirit, and stay away from whatever feeds your harmful desires. God gives you strength to change.
exp.5:2:
This verse says that if someone thinks they are important or better than others, when in reality they are not, they are deceiving themselves. "Thinks himself to be something" means that a person believes they are someone significant, and "deceiveth himself" means that they fall into their own self-deception.

Paul writes to the churches in Galatia. He has just asked that those who are spiritual restore with gentleness someone who has fallen into a fault, and that they help carry one another's burdens. Here he warns that pride gets in the way of that help, because a person who feels superior looks down on others and does not restore them with meekness.

Today, before you correct or judge someone, ask yourself honestly: "Do I think I am better than this person?" Ask God for humility, remember that you too can stumble, and offer help with respect and affection.
exp.0:4:
All glory, that is, all honor and praise, belongs to God the Father, and it will be so forever. The phrase "for ever and ever" is an older way of saying "forever." The word "Amen" means "so be it" or "we agree."

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia. He has just greeted them and reminded them that Jesus gave himself for our sins, according to the will of the Father. This praise flows out of his gratitude for that gift. Right away, Paul expresses his amazement that they are turning away from the gospel, and for this reason his whole letter defends that salvation is by grace.

For today: before we worry about our struggles or arguments, we can begin the day by praising God for what Christ has done. This reminds us that we do not earn salvation ourselves, and that all the glory belongs to God.
exp.4:21:
The explanation says that the Holy Spirit produces a fruit in the life of the believer, just as a healthy tree produces good fruit. It names love (here the word means generous love), joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, and faithfulness, which here can be understood as reliability or trust. It is "fruit" in the singular: one character with several sides.

Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, which were dividing and tearing at one another. He has just listed the works of the flesh, and now he contrasts them with what the Spirit brings forth in those who belong to him. His point is that the Christian life is not sustained by force of rules, but by the work of the Spirit in us.

For today: instead of only trying to control your bad temper or your impatience, ask the Spirit to change you from within. Pray each morning and choose one quality, such as patience, to practice that day.
exp.3:15:
Paul asks a question with a note of pain: "Have I therefore become your enemy because I tell you the truth?" The word "become" in this question means that his relationship with them has changed. Paul does not accuse them in anger; he is puzzled that the relationship has changed so much.

Paul is writing to the believers in Galatia. At first they had received him with great affection, as if he were an angel. Now some teachers were influencing them to depend again on the law to be accepted by God. Paul had spoken to them clearly about the gospel of grace, and that clarity seemed to have cooled their affection.

For today: let us not confuse someone who tells us a hard truth with an enemy. Before we reject a correction, let us humbly examine whether it is true and whether it comes with love. And when it falls to us to speak, let us do it with honesty and kindness.
exp.2:18:
Paul asks a question that anyone would ask: if God's promise to Abraham was already enough, then what is the law for? He answers that it was added because of transgressions. This can be understood in two ways: that the law made the sins visible, or that it restrained them. It lasted until the seed should come, who is Christ. It was ordained through angels and handed down by means of a mediator, which is understood to be Moses.

Paul is writing to the Galatians, who were being persuaded that they had to keep the law in order to be righteous before God. He makes clear that the law does not cancel the promise, but serves a temporary purpose.

For today: when you see your failures, let them lead you to Christ and not to despair. Rest in God's promise, not in your own performance.
exp.5:17:
Paul closes his letter by wishing that the grace of Jesus Christ be with the spirit of the brothers and sisters, that is, with the deepest part of each one. The phrase "your spirit" refers to the spirit of you all.

The closing note "Unto the Galatians written from Rome" is not part of what Paul wrote; it was a note added later in some ancient manuscripts, and many scholars doubt that it is accurate.

Paul is writing to the churches of Galatia, who were being pressed to depend on the law in order to be accepted by God. After firmly defending the truth that we are saved by grace, he ends with a warm blessing. He calls them "brethren," showing affection even after having corrected them sharply.

Today we can remember that grace is not only the beginning of faith but also the air we breathe each day. When you feel weary of striving to earn God's love, rest in his grace, and bless others with that same grace.

sum.0: Paul greets the churches of Galatia and expresses his surprise that they have turned away so quickly from the gospel of Christ's grace to follow a different, distorted message. He affirms that his gospel came through a revelation from Jesus Christ, not from human beings, and he describes how God changed him from a persecutor of the church into a preacher of the faith, for the glory of God.
sum.3: Paul explains that when the right time came, God sent his Son to redeem us and make us children and heirs, not slaves. That is why he is concerned that the Galatians want to go back to depending on the law. Using the allegory of Hagar and Sarah, he teaches that we are children of the promise and of freedom.
sum.2: Paul rebukes the Galatians for wanting to be made complete by works of the law, when they received the Spirit through faith. He teaches them that Abraham was justified by faith and that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law. God's promise still stands, and all who believe in Christ are children of God and heirs.
sum.5: Paul encourages believers to gently restore anyone who falls into sin, to help carry one another's burdens, and to keep doing good without growing weary, sowing for the Spirit. He warns against those who insist on circumcision in order to avoid persecution. He states that he boasts only in the cross of Christ, since what matters is becoming a new creation.
sum.4: Paul urges the Galatians to stand firm in the freedom that Christ gave them, and not to go back under the law or circumcision again, because what counts is faith working through love. He calls them to serve one another, to walk by the Spirit rather than according to the flesh, and to produce the fruit of the Spirit.
sum.1: Paul recounts that he went up to Jerusalem, where the leaders approved his message to the Gentiles and did not require Titus to be circumcised. He then confronted Peter in Antioch for pulling away from the Gentiles out of fear. He teaches that we are made right with God through faith in Christ, not through the works of the law, and that Christ lives within the believer.
